cases.holding: The court affirmed the CINC adjudication, holding that the Kansas Code gives indigent parents a statutory right to appointed counsel in CINC proceedings so the Cooper balancing test is no longer needed, but that a parent who waives counsel and elects to proceed pro se cannot re-invoke the right on the morning of trial and thereby force a continuance.
cases.quote: we refuse to hold that the statutory right to counsel "at any stage of the proceeding" is equivalent to the right at every time

relevance.INP-04: When a court directs that a child-welfare proceeding go forward, the parent's statutory counsel right attaches from the outset, and this case defines when that right can and cannot be re-asserted.
relevance.DEC-05: Once the State files a CINC petition the indigent parent has a statutory right to appointed counsel, so this case fixes the procedural floor at case opening.
relevance.ACT-02: A parent ordered into court-supervised services is entitled to appointed counsel under the Code, subject to the waiver and timeliness limits this case sets.

cases.holding: The court dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction, holding that K.S.A. 38-2273(a) limits appealable CINC orders to the five listed categories and that post-termination permanency orders — including a finding that the agency failed to make reasonable efforts toward adoptive placement and the resulting change of custody to foster parents — are not appealable.
cases.quote: We hold that the Revised Code's appellate jurisdiction statute, K.S.A. 2012 Supp. 38-2273(a), limits what district court decisions may be appealed in a CINC proceeding

relevance.ACT-04: Relatives seeking placement of a child after termination learn here that the post-termination custody rulings they want reviewed are outside the statutory list of appealable orders.
relevance.OUT-03: Post-termination orders awarding custody and consent to adopt to a caregiver are permanency orders that the Court of Appeals has no jurisdiction to review.
relevance.OUT-04: Permanency-hearing requirements continue after termination until adoption or appointment of a permanent custodian, but decisions made at those hearings are unappealable under the Code.
relevance.FAIL-01: This case marks the outer limit of judicial correction of agency permanency decisions in Kansas: after the termination order, appellate review of agency-related findings is unavailable.

cases.holding: The court reversed the CINC adjudication and the termination of parental rights, holding that ICWA's 'qualified expert witness' requirement demands expertise beyond ordinary social-worker credentials, that Kansas courts should consult the ICWA legislative history and the BIA Guidelines, and that the absence of such testimony is not harmless error.
cases.quote: the ICWA heightens the requirements for an expert's qualifications beyond those normally required in a proceeding governed solely by state statutes

relevance.INP-11: Once ICWA applies to a Kansas child, the State must produce a witness with tribal or Indian child-welfare expertise before the child can be placed in foster care or rights terminated.
relevance.FAIL-01: The court reversed both the CINC and termination orders for failure to satisfy ICWA's evidentiary requirements, illustrating judicial correction of an agency-driven outcome.
relevance.FAIL-06: The district court's failure to journalize its CINC findings left no record of ICWA compliance, which the court treated as a defect in the proceedings.
relevance.PMC-05: The absence of any journalized CINC findings in the record is a concrete example of the record-keeping failures that defeat transparency review of child-welfare cases.

cases.holding: Reviewing a collateral order, the court held that a non-Indian biological mother's preference for a non-Indian adoptive family is not, absent a request for anonymity, good cause to deviate from ICWA's placement preferences, and reversed the district court's good-cause finding.
cases.quote: absent a request for anonymity by a biological parent, a parent's placement preference cannot override ICWA's placement factors

relevance.INP-11: This is the leading Kansas statement of how 25 U.S.C. § 1915 placement preferences bind state courts once a child is an 'Indian child,' regardless of the parent's own wishes.
relevance.ACT-04: Placement decisions for an Indian child must follow the statutory order of preference — extended family, then tribal members, then other Indian families — absent genuine good cause.
relevance.FAIL-05: Deviating from ICWA preferences on the strength of a parent's non-Indian placement preference is the kind of placement decision the court identified as unlawful.

cases.holding: The court overruled In re Adoption of Baby Boy L. and abandoned the judicially created 'existing Indian family' doctrine, holding that ICWA applies to a child of both Indian and non-Indian heritage without any threshold inquiry into the family's cultural connection to the tribe.
cases.quote: we hereby overrule Baby Boy L., 231 Kan. 199, and abandon its existing Indian family doctrine

relevance.INP-11: Kansas no longer screens out ICWA cases by asking whether the child came from an 'existing Indian family,' so ICWA attaches whenever the statutory definition of Indian child is met.
relevance.FAIL-05: Abandoning the existing-Indian-family doctrine removes a device that had been used to withhold ICWA's protections from children on the basis of perceived cultural assimilation.

cases.holding: The court affirmed the disposition placing a child in need of care with the noncustodial natural father, holding that the Code permitted that placement without first finding that reasonable efforts had been made to prevent removal from, or to reintegrate the child into, the home from which the child was taken.
cases.quote: the trial court was allowed to place T.S. in the custody of his natural father without first entering a finding of "reasonable efforts."

relevance.DEC-06: Where a fit noncustodial parent is available, Kansas courts may resolve the case without the reasonable-efforts findings that ordinarily precede removal-based dispositions.
relevance.ACT-01: The reasonable-efforts/reintegration machinery is not triggered when the court can place the child with the other parent, which shapes when voluntary service plans are required.
relevance.ACT-02: This case defines when the court must — and need not — order a reintegration plan before making a dispositional custody order.
relevance.ACT-03: The statutory findings that precede removal to agency foster care are not required where custody goes to the noncustodial parent instead.
relevance.OUT-01: Reunification with a parent under the Code can mean placement with the noncustodial parent, not only return to the removal home.

cases.holding: The court held that a parent's relinquishment of parental rights to the Kansas Department for Children and Families is valid without the agency's formal written acceptance, and that the mother's relinquishment was knowing, effective, and attended by the procedural due process she was owed.
cases.quote: formal written acceptance by the Kansas Department for Children and Families (DCF) is not required in order for a parent's relinquishment of parental rights to that agency to be valid

relevance.INP-05: A parent who voluntarily surrenders rights to DCF is bound once the relinquishment is executed, so guardian-initiated contacts with the agency can have irreversible legal effect.
relevance.ACT-02: A parent working a court-ordered case plan may end it by relinquishment, and this case sets out the limited procedural protections that attend that choice.

cases.holding: The court dismissed a grandmother's appeal for lack of jurisdiction, holding that K.S.A. 38-2273(a) permits appeal only of temporary custody, adjudication, disposition, unfitness, and termination orders, and that orders addressing a child's placement — as distinct from custody — are not reviewable.
cases.quote: orders addressing the placement of a child are not dispositional orders, and K.S.A. 38-2273(a) does not vest appellate courts with jurisdiction to review such orders

relevance.ACT-03: A parent or relative unhappy with where the agency places a child in foster care has no appellate remedy under the Code; only custody orders are appealable.
relevance.ACT-04: A grandmother seeking kinship placement must challenge the custody order in time; a later placement dispute is outside appellate jurisdiction.
relevance.OUT-04: Interested parties who want to contest an older youth's continuing placement must find an appealable custody order, because placement rulings alone cannot be reviewed.

cases.holding: The court affirmed termination of parental rights, holding that appellate courts reviewing unfitness findings view all the evidence in the light most favorable to the State, ask only whether a rational factfinder could have found unfitness highly probable, and may not reweigh evidence or reassess witness credibility.
cases.quote: the appellate court does not weigh conflicting evidence, pass on the credibility of witnesses, or redetermine questions of fact

relevance.ACT-02: The parent's compliance or non-compliance with court-ordered services and safety plans is the evidentiary core of the unfitness finding reviewed under this deferential standard.
relevance.OUT-01: Where the record shows the parent rejected the services needed to make return home safe, reintegration findings will be upheld on this deferential review.
relevance.OUT-02: This is the current Kansas Supreme Court statement of the appellate standard governing termination of parental rights, including the unfitness and foreseeable-future elements.
relevance.PMC-06: Any analysis of Kansas termination appeals must account for this highly deferential review, which explains low reversal rates independent of case quality.

cases.holding: The court reversed a termination of parental rights, holding that a party who appears for a termination hearing is presumed to want to participate fully, that the district court must ensure the party can see, hear, speak and consult counsel, and that any waiver of that right must be knowing, voluntary, intelligent and on the record.
cases.quote: a waiver of an appearing party's right to fully and meaningfully participate in a termination of parental rights hearing must be made knowingly, voluntarily, intelligently, and on the record

relevance.OUT-02: This sets the current Kansas due process floor for the conduct of a termination hearing itself, independent of the sufficiency of the evidence.
relevance.FAIL-01: The court vacated a termination order solely because the parent was denied meaningful participation, a clear instance of judicial reversal for procedural error.

cases.holding: The court affirmed Kansas courts' exercise of UCCJEA jurisdiction transferred from California and held that, where minimal due process was afforded, the district court's failure to hold the statutorily required permanency hearing within 30 days did not establish a constitutional due process violation, while stressing that the statutory requirement still binds district courts.
cases.quote: Mother has failed to show a constitutional due process violation resulting from the failure to comply with a Kansas statute

relevance.INP-04: A CINC case can begin in Kansas on a jurisdictional transfer from another state's court, and this case explains when Kansas courts may accept it under the UCCJEA.
relevance.DEC-05: Subject-matter jurisdiction to open or continue a dependency case in Kansas derives from the Code as limited by the UCCJEA, not from the parties' consent.
relevance.OUT-01: A late or missing permanency hearing does not by itself void the reintegration track, though the court reaffirmed that the statutory deadline is mandatory.

cases.case_name: In re Guardianship & Conservatorship of B.H.
cases.holding: The court reversed the Court of Appeals and remanded, holding that the parental preference doctrine governs a parent's petition to terminate a voluntary guardianship absent unfitness or extraordinary circumstances, and that the district court's findings were too sparse to permit appellate review of whether extraordinary circumstances existed.
cases.quote: Because we determine that the district court findings were insufficient to allow proper appellate review, we remand the case to the district court for more complete and specific findings

relevance.INP-05: Parents who voluntarily place children with a guardian during a family crisis retain the parental preference when they later seek the children back, absent unfitness or extraordinary circumstances.
relevance.ACT-01: A voluntary guardianship functions as an alternative to compelled agency intervention, and this case governs how it may later be undone.
relevance.OUT-03: This is the leading recent Kansas authority on terminating a guardianship used as a permanency arrangement and on the findings a court must make.
relevance.OUT-04: The opinion warns against migrating a child's care out of the Code for Care of Children into the Probate Code, which matters for older youth whose permanency is handled by guardianship.

cases.holding: The court reversed a long-term foster care disposition and held that the 'best interests of the child' test in the Code is constitutional only where the court has found by clear and convincing evidence that the parent is unfit or that highly unusual or extraordinary circumstances substantially endanger the child; absent such findings the non-offending parent's right to custody prevails.
cases.quote: In balancing the interests of all parties, the best interests of the child is a factor to be considered and must be given appropriate weight

relevance.INP-05: A parent who comes forward seeking custody of a child already in the system cannot be displaced on best-interests grounds alone without an unfitness or extraordinary-circumstances finding.
relevance.ACT-03: Long-term foster care cannot be ordered over a non-offending parent's objection on a bare best-interests rationale.
relevance.ACT-04: Placement with a relative or third party over a fit parent's objection requires findings beyond the child's preference or comfort in the current home.
relevance.OUT-03: Permanency in a non-parent's home requires unfitness or extraordinary circumstances, not merely a judgment that the child is doing well where she is.
relevance.OUT-05: Where the State cannot show unfitness or extraordinary circumstances as to a particular parent, the child must be returned to that parent rather than kept in care.

cases.holding: The court dismissed a Kansas Open Records Act appeal, holding that a KORA plaintiff must satisfy both KORA's statutory standing requirements and traditional standing, that standing can be lost during litigation, and that loss of standing deprives the courts of jurisdiction.
cases.quote: Baker must establish both (1) any statutory standing requirements imposed by KORA and (2) the traditional requirements of standing

relevance.INP-09: Citizen-initiated records litigation aimed at triggering oversight of an agency or court must clear both statutory and traditional standing hurdles in Kansas.
relevance.FAIL-06: This is the controlling Kansas authority on who may sue when a public agency or court refuses to disclose records, and on how such suits fail on standing rather than the merits.
relevance.PMC-02: Audit-style records requests directed at Kansas public agencies are enforceable only by a requester who can show a continuing, particularized injury.
relevance.PMC-03: Independent panels or advocates seeking agency records must be able to show they personally suffer injury from the denial, not just a general public interest.
relevance.PMC-05: This case sets out the practical limits on KORA as a transparency tool, including the risk that a case becomes unreviewable if the requester's stake disappears.

cases.case_name: T.H. v. University of Kansas Hospital Authority
cases.holding: The court affirmed dismissal of a malpractice suit against a physician who reported suspected sexual abuse, holding that K.S.A. 38-2223(f) immunizes reporters who negligently misdiagnose abuse and that the immunity is lost only if the plaintiff pleads facts supporting actual malice, meaning a specific intent to injure.
cases.quote: In sum, we find that K.S.A. 2015 Supp. 38-2223(f) provides immunity to doctors who negligently misdiagnose child abuse

relevance.INP-01: This is the controlling Kansas construction of the mandatory reporter immunity in K.S.A. 38-2223(f), including the malice exception that defeats it.
relevance.INP-02: The statutory immunity runs to 'anyone' who reports without malice, so voluntary reporters enjoy the same protection the court applied here.
relevance.INP-07: A physician who reports suspected abuse from a clinical encounter is immune even where the diagnosis of abuse turns out to be wrong.
relevance.DEC-03: A family harmed by an erroneous abuse determination generally has no civil remedy against the reporting professional absent pleaded malice.
relevance.ACT-06: Medical professionals who act on a suspicion of abuse in the course of emergency evaluation and examination are shielded from negligence liability for doing so.

cases.holding: The court dismissed in part and affirmed in part, holding that a parent's claim to file an untimely CINC appeal based on ineffective assistance of appointed counsel is governed by the Mathews v. Eldridge balancing test rather than the criminal Ortiz exception, and that on these facts the mother could not appeal the earlier temporary custody and adjudication orders.
cases.quote: any right this mother possessed in filing an untimely appeal based upon the alleged ineffective assistance of mother's appointed counsel must be judged under the balancing tests

relevance.OUT-05: A parent who loses the chance to challenge the adjudication cannot revive it later, so the adjudication effectively fixes whether the case closes as unproven.
relevance.FAIL-01: This case defines the narrow route by which a Kansas parent can obtain appellate correction of CINC orders after the appeal deadline has passed.

cases.holding: The court held the father's challenge to the temporary custody order moot because later adjudication and disposition orders superseded it, but retained the appeal under the public-importance exception and upheld K.S.A. 38-2243(f)(3) — the temporary custody standard — against vagueness and overbreadth attack.
cases.quote: K.S.A. 2011 Supp. 38-2243(f)(3) is neither unconstitutionally vague nor over-broad

relevance.INP-04: This case walks through the ex parte protective custody application and the temporary custody hearing that follow a court-authorized intervention.
relevance.INP-10: It shows the statutory sequence from an ex parte protective custody order to the probable-cause temporary custody hearing that formalizes agency involvement.
relevance.INP-12: The statutory standard authorizing emergency protective custody in Kansas — probable cause that the child's health or welfare may be endangered — survives constitutional challenge.
relevance.DEC-04: The court upheld the probable-cause threshold that Kansas uses to keep a child in temporary custody pending the CINC hearing.
relevance.DEC-05: Temporary custody orders entered at the outset of a petition are appealable but become moot once adjudication and disposition orders are entered.
relevance.ACT-05: Protective custody and temporary custody orders are the Code's principal short-term protective mechanism, and this case validates the standard governing them.
relevance.OUT-05: Because later orders supersede a temporary custody order, challenges to the early phase of the case usually cannot be used to unwind the outcome.

cases.holding: The court affirmed termination of parental rights, holding that ordering a parent to undergo a clinical or substance abuse evaluation in a CINC case does not violate the Fifth Amendment, that non-compliance may be considered in the unfitness analysis, and that a parent's demonstrated unwillingness to participate in treatment may be weighed in deciding whether the State made ICWA 'active efforts.'
cases.quote: we do not find Mother's reluctance to participate in individual therapy meant SFM did not engage in active efforts to persuade her to do so

relevance.INP-11: This is the leading published Kansas decision applying ICWA's 'active efforts' standard and the 25 C.F.R. § 23.2 definition to a state agency's reunification work.
relevance.ACT-01: It holds that a parent may be required to undergo clinical and substance abuse evaluations as part of a service plan without any Fifth Amendment violation.
relevance.ACT-02: Court-ordered evaluations and services are constitutionally permissible, and a parent's refusal to complete them counts against the parent at termination.
relevance.OUT-01: Where reunification fails, the adequacy of the agency's reunification efforts is measured against the parent's own willingness to engage.

cases.holding: The court reversed and remanded the denial of a mother's application to appeal out of time, holding that because a parent's right to counsel in termination proceedings rests on constitutional grounds, the fundamental fairness exception permits an untimely appeal where counsel failed to advise the parent of the 30-day deadline.
cases.quote: we conclude it is proper to apply the fundamental fairness exception to an untimely appeal from a termination order

relevance.FAIL-01: This is the Kansas authority permitting a parent whose appeal was lost to counsel's ineffectiveness to obtain appellate review of a termination order out of time.

cases.holding: The court reversed and remanded a default CINC adjudication entered at a pretrial conference when the father arrived ten minutes late, holding that the blanket notice in the petition did not satisfy K.S.A. 60-255(a) and that due process independently required advance notice that adjudication could occur at that hearing.
cases.quote: Father had a due process right to advance notice that a CINC adjudication could happen at the pending pretrial hearing before such an order could be entered

relevance.INP-04: Once a court proceeding is under way, the parent must receive specific advance notice of any hearing at which the child may be adjudicated.
relevance.DEC-03: A contested finding that a child is in need of care cannot be entered by default without notice satisfying both the civil default statute and due process.
relevance.DEC-05: Generic language in the petition warning of default is not enough; the State must give targeted notice of its intent to seek default adjudication.
relevance.ACT-05: Protective orders and custody consequences that flow from adjudication cannot rest on a default entered without adequate notice.
relevance.OUT-05: The default adjudication was vacated and the case remanded for a contested hearing, showing how procedural defects reopen outcomes.
relevance.FAIL-01: This is a clean example of a Kansas appellate court reversing a CINC adjudication purely for a procedural due process violation.

cases.holding: The court affirmed summary judgment for SRS workers sued for a negligent child abuse investigation preceding a child's death, holding that the reporting and investigation statute creates only a duty to the public at large and that the decision whether to open a file for further investigation is a discretionary function immune under the Kansas Tort Claims Act.
cases.quote: The decision whether to open a file for further investigation is a discretionary function

relevance.INP-01: A report made to SRS creates no enforceable individual duty; the statutory reporting scheme is owed to the public at large.
relevance.INP-02: A reporter who is told the agency will follow up cannot convert that assurance into a special duty running to the child.
relevance.INP-06: Hotline intake decisions are discretionary, so the agency's choice not to act on a call is immune from damages liability in Kansas.
relevance.INP-07: Even where the report comes from a professional source, the agency's decision whether to investigate remains discretionary and immune.
relevance.INP-10: The decision to escalate a screened report into a formal investigation is the discretionary act the court immunized here.
relevance.DEC-01: This is the controlling Kansas authority on liability for screening a report out: there is none, absent an independent duty of care.
relevance.DEC-02: Whether and how to investigate is committed to agency discretion, and internal policy manuals using 'should' create no special duty.
relevance.DEC-06: Choosing a lighter-touch or no-file response to a report is a discretionary judgment protected by K.S.A. 75-6104(d) and (e).
relevance.OUT-06: The case arose from a child's death after SRS declined to open a file, and it forecloses tort recovery on those facts.
relevance.FAIL-04: Families of children who die after a screened-out report have no Kansas tort remedy against the agency workers who made that call.
relevance.PMC-04: Because tort liability is foreclosed, fatality review and external oversight are the only practical accountability mechanisms for screening failures in Kansas.

cases.case_name: Burney v. Kansas Department of Social & Rehabilitation Services
cases.holding: The court reversed a negligence verdict for a substitute teacher who had been investigated for child abuse, holding that SRS owes no duty to an alleged abuser, that there is no special relationship between the agency and a suspect, and that both the decision whether to open a file and the manner of conducting a child abuse investigation are discretionary functions immune under the Kansas Tort Claims Act.
cases.quote: we hold that in investigating child abuse cases, SRS owes no duty to the alleged abuser

relevance.INP-01: A professional accused after a report has no negligence claim against the investigating agency, whatever the quality of the investigation.
relevance.INP-06: The agency's handling of a report, including how it follows up on a call, is discretionary and immune from damages liability.
relevance.INP-08: This case arose from an allegation against a school employee and holds that the educator-suspect is owed no duty by the investigating agency.
relevance.INP-10: The manner of conducting an investigation, not just the decision to open one, is a discretionary function under the Kansas Tort Claims Act.
relevance.DEC-01: Kansas law treats the child protection investigation statutes as creating a public duty only, which bars individual negligence claims arising from screening.
relevance.DEC-02: Investigative technique and thoroughness cannot be second-guessed in tort in Kansas because the manner of investigation is discretionary.
relevance.DEC-03: Someone wrongly named in a substantiated finding cannot sue the agency in negligence for the investigation that produced it.
relevance.FAIL-05: A person who claims the agency singled him out or pursued him improperly has no negligence or malicious prosecution remedy on these facts.
relevance.FAIL-06: The court also held SRS immune for failing to turn over its files to law enforcement, illustrating the breadth of the disclosure immunity.
relevance.PMC-04: Immunity for both screening and investigative conduct means systemic review, not litigation, is the corrective mechanism in Kansas.
relevance.PMC-05: SRS's failure to provide its files to another agency was immunized, which is directly relevant to expectations about records disclosure.

cases.case_name: Roska ex rel. Roska v. Peterson
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that caseworkers who entered a family's home and removed a child without a warrant, court order, or exigent circumstances violated the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments, rejecting the argument that the 'special needs' doctrine excuses the warrant requirement for child welfare removals.
cases.quote: We find no special need that renders the warrant requirement impracticable when social workers enter a home to remove a child, absent exigent circumstances

relevance.INP-03: Where police and caseworkers act together to enter a home, the Fourth Amendment warrant rule applies to the caseworkers just as to the officers.
relevance.INP-12: Emergency protective custody taken by entering the home without a warrant is lawful in this circuit only if genuine exigent circumstances exist.
relevance.DEC-02: An investigation that requires entering the family home needs a warrant, consent, or exigency; the child-protection purpose alone is not enough.
relevance.DEC-04: This is the governing Tenth Circuit rule for the emergency removal decision: no warrant and no exigency means an unconstitutional seizure.
relevance.FAIL-02: This is the leading Tenth Circuit authority for a § 1983 wrongful-removal claim arising from a warrantless, non-exigent removal, which controls in Kansas.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: The court affirmed dismissal on qualified immunity of Fourth Amendment claims brought over a caseworker's warrantless visual body search of a four-year-old at school without parental consent, holding that the law was not clearly established that the special needs doctrine could not justify such a search, and affirmed dismissal of the parents' Fourteenth Amendment claims.
cases.quote: the Does have not shown that Ms. Woodard's search violated clearly established Fourth Amendment law

relevance.INP-07: A caseworker's physical examination of a child's body is a Fourth Amendment search, though qualified immunity may still defeat damages claims.
relevance.INP-08: This is the controlling Tenth Circuit case on caseworkers examining or interviewing children at school without notifying or obtaining consent from parents.
relevance.INP-10: Once a report is escalated to investigation, interviews and examinations of the child at school implicate the Fourth Amendment even though they proceed without a warrant.
relevance.DEC-02: Investigative contact with the child — interview, examination, photographs — is constitutionally regulated conduct, not a free-standing agency prerogative.
relevance.ACT-06: Where an examination of a child is undertaken to assess suspected abuse, its constitutionality is analyzed under the special needs and warrant frameworks discussed here.
relevance.FAIL-02: The circuit's unresolved treatment of the special needs doctrine means many investigative-search claims in Kansas will fail on qualified immunity rather than on the merits.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: In a case beginning with an anonymous hotline call, the court affirmed the denial of qualified immunity to the child welfare specialist and the officer who directed a six-year-old's seizure and transport from school for questioning, while reversing as to the officer who merely transported the child and as to the Fourteenth Amendment familial association claim.
cases.quote: The district court correctly determined that two of the three defendants were not entitled to qualified immunity on the Fourth Amendment unlawful seizure claim

relevance.INP-02: A third-party report is the lawful starting point for agency action, but it does not by itself supply the individualized justification a seizure requires.
relevance.INP-03: The case addresses joint police–child welfare action and separates the liability of the decisionmakers from that of the officer who merely executed the order.
relevance.INP-06: An anonymous hotline call triggered the response here, and the court held it did not justify the seizure that followed.
relevance.INP-08: Removing a child from a classroom for questioning is a Fourth Amendment seizure requiring reasonable justification.
relevance.INP-12: Taking custody of a child for investigative purposes short of a true emergency is a seizure subject to Fourth Amendment reasonableness.
relevance.DEC-04: The decision to take a child into custody must be supported by warrant, probable cause, or reasonable suspicion depending on the circumstances.
relevance.ACT-05: Short-term protective action that restrains a child's liberty must satisfy the Fourth Amendment even when its purpose is protective.
relevance.FAIL-02: This is a recent Tenth Circuit decision allowing a § 1983 unlawful seizure claim against a child welfare worker to proceed past qualified immunity.

cases.case_name: Lowther v. Children, Youth & Families Department
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: The court affirmed qualified immunity for an investigator and county defendants on a warrantless-entry claim, holding that under circuit precedent a reasonable official could believe reasonable suspicion of past abuse justified warrantless entry, so the law was not clearly established to the contrary.
cases.quote: a reasonable investigator or officer could reasonably believe warrantless entry was justified by reasonable suspicion of past abuse

relevance.INP-03: This is the most recent Tenth Circuit treatment of a joint law-enforcement and child-welfare entry into a home during an abuse investigation.
relevance.INP-12: It marks the current outer boundary of warrantless entry in the circuit when officials suspect past — not imminent — abuse.
relevance.DEC-04: Officials deciding whether to enter and remove may rely on reasonable suspicion of past abuse without clearly violating the Fourth Amendment in this circuit.
relevance.ACT-06: Where officials enter to check on a child's medical or physical condition, the exigency analysis in this case governs the constitutionality of that entry.
relevance.FAIL-02: Read together with Roska, this decision shows how narrow the clearly-established path is for a Kansas plaintiff's warrantless-entry claim today.

cases.case_name: Estate of B.I.C. ex rel. C.S.C. v. Gillen
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: In a case arising from the death of a Kansas toddler, the court reversed summary judgment for a Kansas SRS social worker on the state-created danger claim, holding that genuine issues of material fact precluded qualified immunity, while affirming summary judgment on the familial association claims.
cases.quote: We agree that qualified immunity was not appropriate on the state danger-creation claim given genuine issues of material fact

relevance.OUT-06: This is the leading Kansas-origin federal case on liability after a child dies following agency contact, and it identifies the affirmative acts that can support a claim.
relevance.FAIL-02: It shows that the constitutional exposure of Kansas child welfare workers runs to affirmative acts that increase danger, not only to unlawful removals.
relevance.FAIL-04: A social worker who refuses evidence of abuse, deflects to law enforcement, and declares allegations unsubstantiated may face a danger-creation claim if the child is later killed.
relevance.PMC-04: The specific conduct catalogued here — ignored police calls, refused photographic evidence, unsubstantiated findings — is the pattern fatality review is meant to surface.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: The court affirmed the denial of qualified immunity, holding that foster care is a custodial relationship giving rise to a special relationship between the State and the child, which creates a continuing constitutional duty to protect that is violated when officials know of a danger or fail to exercise professional judgment.
cases.quote: foster care is recognized as one of the custodial relationships that creates a special relationship

relevance.ACT-03: Once the State places a child in foster care it assumes an affirmative constitutional duty to protect that child, unlike its duty to children left at home.
relevance.OUT-06: The death or serious injury of a child in foster care is actionable under the special relationship doctrine in this circuit.
relevance.FAIL-04: This supplies the doctrinal basis for § 1983 liability when a child is harmed while under agency supervision in out-of-home placement.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: The court affirmed the denial of qualified immunity to a caseworker who recommended and facilitated a child's placement with an abusive father while withholding known adverse information, holding that on the facts viewed in the child's favor she violated his clearly established substantive due process right to be free from state-created danger.
cases.quote: we conclude that, under Currier, Ms. Patton violated T.D.'s clearly established substantive due process constitutional right to be free of a state official's creation of danger from a private actor

relevance.ACT-03: A caseworker's placement recommendation that puts a child with a known dangerous caregiver can itself be the constitutional violation.
relevance.OUT-06: Serious injury to a child following a caseworker's affirmative placement recommendation supports a substantive due process claim in this circuit.
relevance.FAIL-04: This is the clearest recent Tenth Circuit statement that a caseworker's affirmative conduct, including withholding known risk information, defeats qualified immunity.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause requires at least clear and convincing evidence before a State may terminate parental rights, vacated the judgment approving New York's preponderance standard, and left States free to adopt any burden at or above that level.
cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

relevance.OUT-02: This is the federal constitutional floor for the standard of proof in every termination of parental rights case, including Kansas proceedings under K.S.A. 38-2269.

cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that due process does not require appointment of counsel for indigent parents in every parental termination proceeding, leaving the decision in the first instance to the trial court applying the Mathews v. Eldridge factors subject to appellate review, and affirmed on the facts.
cases.quote: neither can we say that the Constitution requires the appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding

relevance.OUT-02: This is the federal baseline on appointed counsel at termination; Kansas exceeds it by statute, and Kansas courts apply its Mathews framework to related counsel questions.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that an unwed father was entitled as a matter of due process to a hearing on his fitness before his children could be taken from him, and that Illinois' presumption of unfitness applied only to unwed fathers denied him equal protection.
cases.quote: as a matter of due process of law, Stanley was entitled to a hearing on his fitness as a parent before his children were taken from him

relevance.INP-12: State action separating a child from a parent must be accompanied by a hearing on that parent's fitness rather than a categorical presumption.
relevance.DEC-04: Even in an emergency framework, the Constitution requires an individualized fitness determination before the separation is made permanent.
relevance.FAIL-02: This is the foundational federal holding that removal without an individualized hearing violates due process, on which wrongful-removal claims ultimately rest.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court affirmed judgment for the county, holding that the Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative duty on a State to protect a child from private violence merely because caseworkers knew of the danger, while noting that a custodial relationship such as state-operated foster care might be different.
cases.quote: nothing in the language of the Due Process Clause itself requires the State to protect the life, liberty, and property of its citizens against invasion by private actors

relevance.DEC-01: Screening a report out or closing it as unfounded creates no federal constitutional liability even if the child is later harmed by a parent.
relevance.OUT-06: A child's death at a parent's hands after agency contact does not, without more, establish a federal due process violation.
relevance.FAIL-04: This is the controlling federal limit on agency liability for failure to protect, and it drives the state-created danger and special relationship exceptions the Tenth Circuit applies.
relevance.PMC-04: Because federal constitutional liability is foreclosed for pure inaction, fatality review commissions carry the accountability function that litigation cannot.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court rejected all challenges to the Indian Child Welfare Act, upholding Congress's authority to enact it, reversing on the anticommandeering claims, and vacating for lack of standing the equal protection and nondelegation challenges to the placement preferences.
cases.quote: the bottom line is that we reject all of petitioners' challenges to the statute, some on the merits and others for lack of standing

relevance.INP-11: ICWA remains fully enforceable against Kansas courts and agencies, including its notice, active efforts, expert witness and placement preference requirements.
relevance.FAIL-03: State officials cannot decline to apply ICWA on anticommandeering grounds, so non-compliance is a federal compliance failure rather than a contested legal question.
relevance.FAIL-05: The equal protection challenge to ICWA's placement preferences was left unresolved for lack of standing, so the preferences continue to govern placements.
relevance.PMC-01: Federal monitoring of state ICWA compliance rests on a statute the Court has now sustained against structural constitutional attack.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court reversed, holding that the 'reasonable efforts' requirement of 42 U.S.C. § 671(a)(15) in the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act creates neither a right enforceable by beneficiaries under § 1983 nor an implied private right of action.
cases.quote: We conclude that 42 U. S. C. § 671(a)(15) neither confers an enforceable private right on its beneficiaries nor creates an implied cause of action on their behalf

relevance.INP-09: Federal child welfare plan requirements are enforced through the Secretary's oversight and funding levers, not by private suit, which is why audits and reviews matter.
relevance.DEC-06: A family that believes the agency should have offered prevention services instead of removing has no federal private remedy for a reasonable-efforts shortfall.
relevance.FAIL-03: Failure to meet federal IV-E plan requirements is remediable through federal administrative and funding mechanisms rather than private litigation.
relevance.PMC-01: CFSR and related federal review processes are the operative enforcement channel precisely because § 671(a)(15) is not privately enforceable.
relevance.PMC-02: Financial and program audits by federal overseers, not beneficiary lawsuits, are the sanction for state non-compliance with IV-E plan requirements.
relevance.PMC-03: Citizen review panels and similar bodies supply scrutiny that private enforcement litigation cannot, given this holding.
relevance.PMC-04: Any accountability model for Kansas must account for the absence of a private federal remedy for reasonable-efforts failures.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court vacated and remanded, holding that individuals have no § 1983 right to require a State's 'substantial compliance' with a federal Social Security Act program, and that courts must analyze each statutory provision separately rather than treating a multifaceted funding scheme as a single source of rights.
cases.quote: The Court of Appeals erred not only in finding that individuals have an enforceable right to substantial compliance

relevance.INP-09: Systemic non-compliance found by federal audit does not translate into individually enforceable rights, so oversight findings are the operative lever.
relevance.FAIL-03: A State's aggregate failure to meet federal performance standards is not itself privately actionable; each provision must be examined for rights-creating language.
relevance.PMC-01: CFSR-style performance measurement is designed for federal administrative enforcement, which this decision confirms is the primary channel.
relevance.PMC-02: Audit findings of program shortfalls support federal corrective action and penalties rather than beneficiary damages or injunctions.
relevance.PMC-03: Review panels evaluating agency performance operate in the space this decision leaves open, since courts will not order 'substantial compliance.'
relevance.PMC-06: Cross-state compliance scoring must be framed as an oversight and policy tool, because courts will not enforce aggregate compliance as a right.

cases.holding: The court reversed the Court of Appeals and affirmed the deprived-child adjudication, holding that due process requires appointed counsel for an indigent parent on a case-by-case basis — where the parent cannot properly present the case and faces a substantial possibility of losing custody permanently or of prolonged separation — and that a refusal to appoint counsel must be explained on the record.
cases.quote: the district court should safeguard the due process rights of an indigent parent and have counsel appointed at the expense of the county when the circumstances appear to require it

relevance.INP-04: This is the Kansas Supreme Court source of the balancing test that governed a parent's right to appointed counsel once a child-welfare proceeding was opened against her, the test In re J.A.H. later describes as superseded by statute.
relevance.DEC-05: When the State files a petition the district court must consider, on the record, whether the indigent parent's circumstances require appointed counsel, and must state grounds for any refusal.

cases.case_name: In re Adoption of Baby Boy L.
cases.holding: The court affirmed a decree of adoption, holding that ICWA did not apply because the child had never been part of an existing Indian family unit and that adoption without the putative father's consent under K.S.A. 59-2102(2) did not violate due process or equal protection — a holding expressly overruled, and the existing-Indian-family doctrine abandoned, by In re A.J.S., 288 Kan. 429 (2009).
cases.quote: the Act is concerned with the removal of Indian children from an existing Indian family unit and the resultant breakup of the Indian family

relevance.INP-11: This is the overruled source of the 'existing Indian family' exception that Kansas courts used for 27 years to hold ICWA inapplicable to children of Indian heritage; it is no longer good law after In re A.J.S. (2009).
relevance.FAIL-05: The doctrine announced here withheld ICWA's protections from a child on the basis of the family's perceived lack of tribal connection, and its abandonment is the corrective In re A.J.S. supplies.

cases.holding: The court affirmed the CINC adjudication, holding that the Sixth Amendment Confrontation Clause does not apply in CINC proceedings, that a child's hearsay statements were admissible under K.S.A. 60-460(a) even though the State did not call her in its case in chief, and that the district judge's standing offer to summon the child for cross-examination satisfied whatever confrontation right due process supplied.
cases.quote: Any right that a civil litigant can claim to confrontation and cross-examination is grounded in the Due Process Clauses of the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments

relevance.DEC-03: A finding that a child is in need of care may rest on the child's out-of-court statements relayed by a counselor, investigator and detective, so long as the declarant is made available for cross-examination.
relevance.DEC-05: Once a CINC petition is filed the case is civil, not criminal, so the parent's confrontation protections come from due process rather than the Sixth Amendment.
relevance.OUT-05: A parent who declines the court's offer to call the child for cross-examination cannot later obtain dismissal of the adjudication on confrontation grounds.

cases.holding: The court affirmed the CINC adjudication, holding that clear and convincing evidence in Kansas means evidence sufficient to establish that the truth of the facts asserted is highly probable, disapproving all contrary holdings, and that an appellate court reviewing such a determination asks only whether a rational factfinder could have found it highly probable on the evidence viewed most favorably to the State.
cases.quote: We agree with those courts that have essentially defined clear and convincing evidence as that which is sufficient to establish that the truth of the facts asserted is "highly probable."

relevance.DEC-03: This is the load-bearing Kansas definition of the burden the State must carry to obtain a finding that a child is in need of care.
relevance.OUT-05: Where the State's proof does not make the required facts highly probable, the adjudication fails and the case cannot proceed on that basis.
relevance.FAIL-01: The deferential standard of review announced here — no reweighing of evidence, no credibility redetermination — governs every Kansas appeal seeking reversal of a CINC or termination order.

cases.case_name: In re Adoption of Baby Girl P.
cases.holding: The court reversed the termination of a natural father's parental rights and the Court of Appeals' affirmance, holding that the adoption petitioners failed to prove any K.S.A. 59-2136(h)(1) factor by clear and convincing evidence and that the child's best interests cannot alone justify termination, and remanded for a custodial transition to the father not to exceed 30 days.
cases.quote: As with stepparent adoptions, the best interest of the child may not be the sole basis for terminating a parent's rights

relevance.INP-05: A natural father who comes forward and asserts his rights before an adoption is final is entitled to the parental preference, not to a comparison of households.
relevance.OUT-02: This is the Kansas Supreme Court's statement of the clear-and-convincing burden an adoption petitioner bears before a natural father's rights may be terminated.
relevance.OUT-03: Permanency with prospective adoptive parents cannot be justified by the strength of the bonds formed during litigation when the statutory grounds are unproven.

cases.holding: The court affirmed the district court's refusal to set aside a finalized adoption, holding that an unwed father of a newborn who did not grasp his fleeting opportunity to commit to parenting during the pregnancy acquired no protected liberty interest, so the absence of notice to him did not make the adoption void, and rejecting his fraud and equal protection theories.
cases.quote: We hold that M.P. did not have a liberty interest in a relationship with A.A.T. and that the State did not deny him the opportunity to establish such a relationship

relevance.OUT-02: This is the leading Kansas authority on an unwed father's notice and consent rights when adoption is the permanency outcome, and on how quickly that opportunity closes.

cases.case_name: Gloria G. v. State Department of Social & Rehabilitation Services
cases.holding: The court reversed a jury verdict against SRS and entered judgment for the agency, holding that SRS's decision to remove a child from a foster home was a discretionary act immune from liability under the discretionary function exception of the Kansas Tort Claims Act, K.S.A. 75-6104(e).
cases.quote: SRS is immune from liability because the removal of A. from the foster care home by SRS was a discretionary act under K.S.A. 75-6104(e)

relevance.DEC-01: This is the Kansas Supreme Court source of the discretionary-function immunity that the Court of Appeals later extended in Beebe to the decision whether to open a file at all.
relevance.DEC-02: Agency case decisions about a child — including how and when to act on what the agency knows — are judged under the discretionary-function framework this case establishes.
relevance.DEC-06: Choosing one course of agency response over another is a judgment the legislature placed beyond tort review, even when the agency departs from its own manual.

cases.case_name: C.J.W. ex rel. L.W. v. State
cases.holding: The court reversed summary judgment for the State in a suit by a 12-year-old assaulted in juvenile detention, holding that the State owed him a duty under Restatement (Second) of Torts §§ 315, 319 and 320 to warn of and protect against a known dangerous detainee, that the discretionary function exception did not immunize breach of that legally imposed duty, and that controverted facts precluded summary judgment.
cases.quote: Children who are taken into custody should be protected from others in custody

relevance.ACT-03: This is the Kansas-law counterpart to the federal special-relationship cases: once the State takes a child into its custody it owes that child an affirmative duty of protection.
relevance.OUT-06: A child seriously harmed while in state custody has a Kansas tort claim where the State knew of the danger, notwithstanding the Tort Claims Act.
relevance.FAIL-04: Where a mandatory legal duty to protect a child in custody exists, the discretionary function exception does not shield the agency from damages liability.

cases.case_name: Bolyard ex rel. Bolyard v. Kansas Department of Social & Rehabilitation Services
cases.holding: The court affirmed summary judgment for SRS and its caseworker, holding that placing children who were in SRS temporary custody with their mother, and the means chosen to monitor that placement, were discretionary functions immune under the Kansas Tort Claims Act because no clearly defined mandatory duty or guideline required a different course.
cases.quote: The discretionary function exception is applicable only when no clearly defined mandatory duty or guideline exists which the government agency is required to follow

relevance.DEC-06: The agency's choice of a less restrictive response — placing children with a parent rather than in agency foster care — is discretionary and immune absent a mandatory guideline.
relevance.OUT-01: Placing a child in agency custody back with a parent is the archetypal discretionary judgment, and the adequacy of the agency's supervision of that placement is not reviewable in tort.

cases.holding: The court reversed the denial of a natural mother's petition to terminate a voluntary guardianship and overruled In re Marriage of Criqui, holding that the best-interests test does not apply, and the parental preference doctrine controls, in a custody dispute between a nonparent and a parent who has not been found unfit, absent highly unusual or extraordinary circumstances.
cases.quote: absent highly unusual or extraordinary circumstances it has no application in determining whether a parent, not found to be unfit, is entitled to custody as against a third-party nonparent

relevance.INP-05: A parent who voluntarily hands a child to a caregiver during a crisis does not forfeit the parental preference when she later asks for the child back.
relevance.ACT-04: A relative or kin caregiver cannot retain a child over a fit parent's objection on the strength of the child's attachment or comfort in the current home.
relevance.OUT-03: This is the leading Kansas statement of the parental preference doctrine and of the extraordinary-circumstances showing required before guardianship becomes a permanency arrangement.

cases.case_name: State, Department of Social & Rehabilitation Services v. Paillet
cases.holding: The court reversed a grandparent visitation order, holding that K.S.A. 38-129 was unconstitutional as applied because the courts below failed to give the fit mother's decision the presumption and special weight Troxel requires and because the grandparents did not carry their burden on either statutory element, while declining to hold the statute facially invalid.
cases.quote: we do not find K.S.A. 38-129 to be unconstitutional on its face but only in its application in the present case

relevance.INP-05: When relatives invoke a statute to obtain access to a child over a fit parent's objection, the parent's own judgment is presumed correct and must be given special weight.
relevance.ACT-04: Grandparents and other kin seeking court-ordered contact or placement bear the burden of proof, and a fit parent's limits on that contact do not forfeit the presumption in the parent's favor.

cases.holding: In a suit by day care operators against state and local health officials, the court affirmed judgment for most defendants but reversed summary judgment for KDHE on the abuse-of-process and malicious-prosecution claims, holding that the Kansas Tort Claims Act's discretionary function exception applies only where no mandatory duty or guideline exists and confers no immunity for maliciously prosecuting a citizen.
cases.quote: The government has no power or grant of immunity under the KTCA to maliciously prosecute a citizen of the state

relevance.DEC-02: This is the Kansas Supreme Court framework for the discretionary-function exception that Burney and Beebe apply to child protection investigations, including its limit where a legal duty exists.
relevance.FAIL-05: A person who claims a state agency pursued enforcement against him maliciously has a remedy in Kansas notwithstanding the Tort Claims Act, unlike a claim of mere negligent investigation.

cases.holding: The court affirmed summary judgment for the Register of Deeds, holding that KORA's exceptions to disclosure are narrowly construed with the burden on the agency opposing disclosure, but that where releasing personal identifiers would not significantly serve KORA's purpose nondisclosure is favored and the requester may be charged the reasonable cost of redaction.
cases.quote: narrowly interpreted, and the burden is on the public agency opposing disclosure

relevance.FAIL-06: This is the Kansas Supreme Court's allocation of the burden when a public agency refuses to release records: the agency, not the requester, must justify the withholding.
relevance.PMC-05: A transparency requester in Kansas benefits from a presumption of openness but may lawfully be charged redaction costs and denied personal identifiers that do not serve KORA's purpose.

notes: Every case listed was retrieved from the CourtListener v4 API in this session and its opinion text read; each quote was programmatically verified as an exact substring of the retrieved opinion text after whitespace and curly-quote normalization. All quotes are from majority/lead opinions (CourtListener opinion type 020lead or 010combined); no syllabus paragraph, dissent, or concurrence was quoted. Where a Kansas opinion carries a 'SYLLABUS BY THE COURT', the quoted language was taken from the body of the opinion, not the syllabus.
No unpublished or memorandum decisions were used. Every state case is a published Kansas Supreme Court or published Kansas Court of Appeals opinion.

The existing layers.case_law.key_cases entries in the KS node files are keyword-matched noise with synthetic citations (e.g. 'Kansas Supreme Court Case 119012 (2025)' pointing at law.justia.com). None survived verification: 'In re Mason' and 'In re Adoption of Baby Boy S.' as listed could not be confirmed as on-point child-welfare authority and were discarded. Nothing from those lists is carried into this brief.

Kansas has no reported appellate decision testing the constitutionality of a child abuse and neglect central registry or the due-process rights attached to an administrative 'substantiated' finding. DEC-03 is therefore built from the proof standard (In re B.D.-Y.), the judicial-notice/default cases (In re J.L.), and the immunity/no-duty line (Burney; T.H.). Practitioners challenging a DCF substantiation in Kansas should expect to litigate under the Kansas Judicial Review Act and K.A.R. Agency 30 rather than under a body of case law.

DEC-06 (Differential/Alternative Response) has no on-point Kansas appellate authority. The entry is built from the discretionary-function immunity for the decision not to open a file (Beebe), the reasonable-efforts flexibility recognized in In re T.S., and the federal rule that reasonable efforts are not privately enforceable (Suter v. Artist M.).

OUT-04 (Extended foster care / aging out) has no Kansas appellate decision construing the Chafee or FCSIAA-funded extended-care provisions or K.S.A. 38-2203(b) custody past age 18. The cases mapped (In re N.A.C., In re N.E., In re Guardianship & Conservatorship of B.H.) govern the jurisdictional and permanency framework within which an older youth's placement is decided; they are the closest available Kansas authority and no case squarely addresses aging-out rights.

ACT-05 (Protective Order) has no Kansas child-welfare appellate case on no-contact or abuser-removal orders entered under the Revised Kansas Code for Care of Children. The mapped cases address the protective custody / temporary custody machinery (In re A.E.S.), the notice due before protective adjudication (In re J.L.), and the Fourth Amendment limits on protective seizures (Halley v. Huckaby). Kansas practice on protective orders as such runs through the Protection from Abuse Act, K.S.A. 60-3101 et seq., which has not generated on-point child-welfare precedent.

FAIL-03 and PMC-01 through PMC-04 have no Kansas state authority. They are given the federal standard: Suter v. Artist M. (no private enforcement of the IV-E reasonable-efforts plan requirement) and Blessing v. Freestone (no right to a State's 'substantial compliance' with a federal Social Security Act program), plus Haaland v. Brackeen for ICWA compliance. The practical consequence for families and lawyers is that CFSR findings, Single Audit Act results, and Citizen Review Panel reports are oversight instruments, not causes of action.

No reported Kansas or Tenth Circuit decision addresses children who go missing from foster care. That topic is not separately mapped; ACT-03 and OUT-06 carry the nearest authority on the State's custodial duty (Schwartz v. Booker; T.D. v. Patton).

Kansas child-welfare tort exposure is unusually narrow. Beebe v. Fraktman and Burney v. Kansas SRS together hold that (1) the reporting/investigation statutes create a duty to the public at large only, (2) the decision whether to open a file is a discretionary function, and (3) the manner of conducting an abuse investigation is also a discretionary function immune under K.S.A. 75-6104(d) and (e). A Kansas plaintiff harmed by a negligent investigation will ordinarily have to proceed under 42 U.S.C. section 1983 in the Tenth Circuit rather than in state tort.

For section 1983 removal and investigation claims, the Tenth Circuit is the controlling federal forum for Kansas. Roska (2002) and Lowther (2024) should be read together: Roska establishes that warrantless, non-exigent entry to remove a child violates the Fourth Amendment, while Lowther holds that reasonable suspicion of past abuse can make warrantless entry at least not clearly unlawful, so qualified immunity frequently defeats such claims today. Doe v. Woodard likewise resolves the searching of a child at school on clearly-established grounds without deciding whether the special needs doctrine applies, leaving the underlying question open in this circuit.

Estate of B.I.C. ex rel. C.S.C. v. Gillen arises from Kansas facts (a Kansas SRS social worker and the 2008 death of a 23-month-old in Kansas) and is the most directly transferable federal authority in this brief for child-fatality accountability in this jurisdiction. A later appeal in the same litigation (761 F.3d 1099 (10th Cir. 2014)) was not retrieved or relied on here.

Citation form notes: several recent Kansas Supreme Court clusters (In re P.R., In re N.E., In re D.G., In re A.S., In re A.A.-F., In re Guardianship & Conservatorship of B.H., In re Adoption of C.L., Baker v. Hayden) carry only a Pacific Reporter citation in CourtListener, so the court designator '(Kan. YYYY)' is supplied. Lassiter's date_decided reflects the CourtListener cluster date of 1981-08-28 (denial of rehearing); the opinion itself issued June 1, 1981.

In re B.D.-Y. is the load-bearing Kansas case for this entire dataset: it defines 'clear and convincing evidence' as 'highly probable' for both CINC adjudication and termination, disapproves all contrary prior Kansas holdings, and supplies the appellate standard restated in In re D.G. (2024). Any Kansas node that turns on a burden of proof should cite it.

In re A.S. (2024) is the newest structural due-process rule in Kansas termination practice: a parent who appears must be able to see, hear, speak, and consult counsel, and any waiver must be knowing, voluntary, intelligent, and on the record. It is likely to be the most frequently invoked recent authority for families challenging a termination hearing's conduct.

Appellate jurisdiction is a recurring trap in Kansas CINC practice. In re N.A.C. (2014) and In re N.E. (2022) together hold that K.S.A. 38-2273(a) lists only five appealable order types, that post-termination permanency orders are unappealable, and that placement orders (as distinct from custody orders) cannot be reviewed at all. Relatives, kin, and foster parents should be advised that the practical window for appellate review closes at the termination order.
Research budget: approximately 75 CourtListener API requests were used, paced at roughly one every two seconds. No source other than CourtListener was fetched.

Missing (for a later pass): In re J.D.C., 284 Kan. 155, 159 P.3d 974 (2007) — the load-bearing Kansas Supreme Court case on a parent's right to counsel and on ineffective-assistance claims in CINC proceedings, decided under the Mathews v. Eldridge balancing framework. Both In re L.B. and In re J.A.H., which the brief does include, are built directly on it; citing the derivative cases without the source leaves INP-04, DEC-05 and FAIL-01 resting on secondary authority. Its existence and citation are confirmed from the opinions retrieved here.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Adoption of Baby Girl P., 291 Kan. 424, 242 P.3d 1168 (2010) — the Kansas Supreme Court's statement of the natural father's rights in a private adoption, the clear-and-convincing standard, and the expedited-custodial-transition remedy. In re Adoption of C.L. (2018) rests on it (the constitutional sentence the brief quotes is drawn from it), and In re D.G. (2024) cites it for the no-reweighing rule. It should anchor OUT-02 instead of being invisible.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Adoption of A.A.T., 287 Kan. 590, 196 P.3d 1180 (2008) — the leading Kansas authority on an unwed father's notice and consent rights in a private adoption and on the burden borne by the adoption petitioner. In re Adoption of B.B.M. expressly relies on it for the very burden allocation the brief attributes to B.B.M. alone. Missing from OUT-02 and OUT-03.

Missing (for a later pass): G. v. State Dept. of SRS, 251 Kan. 179, 833 P.2d 979 (1992) — the Kansas Supreme Court decision holding that an SRS decision about a child's placement falls within the discretionary-function exception of the Kansas Tort Claims Act. This is the Supreme Court source that Beebe v. Fraktman applies; the brief rests a load-bearing immunity rule entirely on two Court of Appeals cases. Belongs at DEC-01, DEC-02, DEC-06 and ACT-03.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Guardianship of Williams, 254 Kan. 814, 869 P.2d 661 (1994) — the leading Kansas statement of the parental preference doctrine and of what qualifies as 'extraordinary circumstances' sufficient to displace a fit parent. In re Guardianship & Conservatorship of B.H. (2019) is an application of it and In re M.M.L. turns on the same doctrine. Its absence weakens INP-05, ACT-04 and OUT-03.

Missing (for a later pass): Lindenman v. Umscheid, 255 Kan. 610, 875 P.2d 964 (1994) — the Kansas Supreme Court's framework for the Kansas Tort Claims Act discretionary-function exception and for malicious prosecution against a state agency; Burney applies it expressly. Without it, DEC-01, DEC-02 and FAIL-05 rest entirely on intermediate-appellate authority.

Missing (for a later pass): Kansas Dept. of SRS v. Paillet, 270 Kan. 646, 16 P.3d 962 (2001) — Kansas Supreme Court authority on the agency's duty, and the limits of that duty, in connection with foster placement and the information supplied to caregivers. It is the natural Kansas-law counterpart to Schwartz v. Booker and T.D. v. Patton at ACT-03, OUT-06 and FAIL-04; as the brief stands there is no state-law authority at all on the State's duty to a child already in its custody.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Adoption of Baby Boy L., 231 Kan. 199, 643 P.2d 168 (1982) — the decision In re A.J.S. overruled. A brief presenting A.J.S. as abandoning the existing-Indian-family doctrine should cite the overruled case in full with its negative history stated, both so the overruling is explicit and so a researcher does not pick Baby Boy L. up from a stale source. At present it appears only inside a quotation.

GAP-CLOSING PASS (2026-09-20): all eight authorities named by the verifier were searched by citation on CourtListener (court=kan), retrieved, and read in full. All eight exist and are now added. Two of them, however, do not hold what the verifier's description said, and the entries added state what the opinions actually decide. Thirteen cases were added in total; the brief now carries 49 distinct cases, above the 20-40 target, because Kansas doctrine on agency immunity, parental preference and ICWA each requires both the Supreme Court source and its Court of Appeals applications. Every one of the 42 nodes now carries between two and six cases.

Added In re J.D.C., 284 Kan. 155 (2007) for DEC-03, DEC-05, OUT-05: retrieved and read in full — CORRECTION TO THE VERIFIER'S NOTE. In re J.D.C. is not a right-to-counsel or ineffective-assistance case. It holds that the Sixth Amendment Confrontation Clause does not apply in CINC proceedings, that a child's hearsay statements are admissible under K.S.A. 60-460(a) without the State calling her in its case in chief, and that the trial judge's standing offer to summon the child satisfied any due process confrontation right. It is valuable Kansas authority on the evidentiary basis for an adjudication, but it does not support INP-04 or FAIL-01 and is not mapped there.

Added In re Cooper, 230 Kan. 57, 631 P.2d 632 (1981) for INP-04 and DEC-05: this, not In re J.D.C., is the Kansas Supreme Court source of the parent's right-to-counsel doctrine in child-welfare proceedings — the 'Cooper balancing test' that In re J.A.H. (2007) says the statute has now displaced. The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals (5 Kan. App. 2d 584, 621 P.2d 437 (1980), which had required counsel whenever custody was removed even temporarily) and adopted a case-by-case due process test. Retrieving it supplies the missing source authority the verifier was looking for.

Added In re B.D.-Y., 286 Kan. 686, 187 P.3d 594 (2008) for DEC-03, OUT-05 and FAIL-01: the brief's own notes called this the load-bearing Kansas case on the standard of proof and standard of review, but it had never been retrieved or entered as a case. It is now verified and mapped.

Added In re Adoption of Baby Girl P., 291 Kan. 424 (2010) for INP-05, OUT-02 and OUT-03: verified as described by the verifier — the court reversed termination of the natural father's rights for failure of clear-and-convincing proof of any K.S.A. 59-2136(h)(1) factor, held best interests cannot alone terminate rights, and ordered a custodial transition not to exceed 30 days. The quote is taken from the majority (Rosen, J.); the Luckert concurrence was excluded.

Added In re Adoption of A.A.T., 287 Kan. 590 (2008) for OUT-02: PARTIAL CORRECTION. The holding is that an unwed father of a newborn who failed to grasp his fleeting opportunity to commit to parenting during the pregnancy had no liberty interest, so lack of notice did not void the finalized adoption; the opinion discusses the petitioner's burden but does not hold on it, and the combined text carries three dissents (Nuss, Beier, Rosen) from which nothing was quoted. Mapped to OUT-02 only; it does not support OUT-03, which concerns guardianship and kinship permanency.

Added Gloria G. v. State Department of Social & Rehabilitation Services, 251 Kan. 179 (1992) for DEC-01, DEC-02 and DEC-06: this is the Supreme Court source of the discretionary-function immunity rule that Beebe and Burney apply, as the verifier said. It is not mapped to ACT-03, which already carries six cases including the stronger Kansas custodial-duty authority added in this pass. CourtListener holds two clusters for this case (7968998 and 2607429); the Kansas Reports cluster was used.

Added In re Guardianship of Williams, 254 Kan. 814 (1994) for INP-05, ACT-04 and OUT-03: verified as described — the leading Kansas statement of the parental preference doctrine, overruling In re Marriage of Criqui and holding the best-interests test inapplicable against a parent not found unfit absent highly unusual or extraordinary circumstances.

Added Lindenman v. Umscheid, 255 Kan. 610 (1994) for DEC-02 and FAIL-05: verified as described — the Supreme Court's discretionary-function framework ('applicable only when no clearly defined mandatory duty or guideline exists') plus the holding that the KTCA grants no immunity to maliciously prosecute a citizen. The facts are day-care licensing enforcement, not a CPS investigation, which is stated here so no reader assumes a child-protection holding.

Added State, Department of Social & Rehabilitation Services v. Paillet, 270 Kan. 646 (2001) for INP-05 and ACT-04: CORRECTION TO THE VERIFIER'S NOTE. Paillet is a grandparent-visitation case decided under Troxel v. Granville; it holds K.S.A. 38-129 unconstitutional as applied where the courts below failed to give a fit parent's decision special weight. It says nothing about the agency's duty in foster placement or about information supplied to caregivers, and it is therefore not mapped to ACT-03, OUT-06 or FAIL-04.

Added C.J.W. ex rel. L.W. v. State, 253 Kan. 1, 853 P.2d 4 (1993) for ACT-03, OUT-06 and FAIL-04: this is the Kansas Supreme Court authority the verifier wanted from Paillet and did not get. A 12-year-old was assaulted while in state juvenile custody; the court held the State owed him a Restatement duty to warn and protect, that the discretionary function exception does not immunize breach of a legally imposed duty, and reversed summary judgment. It is the state-law counterpart to Schwartz v. Booker and T.D. v. Patton, and it closes the brief's acknowledged gap of having no Kansas authority on the State's duty to a child already in its custody. The quote is from the lead opinion (Holmes, C.J.), not the McFarland concurrence.

Added Bolyard ex rel. Bolyard v. Kansas Department of Social & Rehabilitation Services, 259 Kan. 447 (1996) for DEC-06 and OUT-01: the Supreme Court companion to Gloria G., holding that both the decision to place children in SRS temporary custody with a parent and the means of monitoring that placement are discretionary and immune absent a mandatory guideline. Read with C.J.W. it marks the line in Kansas between immunized placement judgment and an enforceable mandatory duty to protect.

Added In re Adoption of Baby Boy L., 231 Kan. 199, 643 P.2d 168 (1982) for INP-11 and FAIL-05, with its negative history stated in the holding field: it was expressly overruled and its existing-Indian-family doctrine abandoned by In re A.J.S., 288 Kan. 429 (2009). It is included so the overruling is explicit on the face of this brief and no researcher picks it up from a stale source. It must never be cited as current Kansas law.

Added Data Tree, LLC v. Meek, 279 Kan. 445, 109 P.3d 1226 (2005) for FAIL-06 and PMC-05: FAIL-06 and PMC-05 previously had only one mapped case each in node_map. Data Tree is the Kansas Supreme Court's allocation of the KORA burden — exceptions narrowly interpreted, burden on the agency opposing disclosure — subject to redaction costs and the personal-privacy exception. Read with Baker v. Hayden (standing) it gives Kansas transparency work both its burden rule and its jurisdictional trap.

node_map repair: several cases already carried relevance sentences for nodes that node_map omitted. Those mappings are now reflected, with no change to any existing case entry: In re M.F. and Burney added to FAIL-06 and PMC-05; In re J.A.H., In re A.A.-F. and In re J.L. added to INP-04; In re N.A.C., In re N.E. and In re Guardianship & Conservatorship of B.H. added to OUT-04, which was previously empty.

Authority searched and NOT added: no Kansas appellate decision on extended foster care or aging out could be located. A targeted search of both kan and kanctapp for K.S.A. 38-2203, extended custody past age 18, and Chafee/FCSIAA transitional services returned only two hits, neither on point (Cosgrove v. Kansas SRS, 14 Kan. App. 2d 217 (1990), and In re Cooper). OUT-04 therefore continues to rest on the jurisdictional and permanency cases noted above, and there is no U.S. Supreme Court standard on aging out to substitute — the Chafee program, like the IV-E plan requirements in Suter v. Artist M., is enforced administratively and not by private suit.

Budget note for this pass: approximately 40 additional CourtListener requests were made (13 citation/keyword searches, 16 opinion-text retrievals, 13 cluster-metadata retrievals), paced at one request every two seconds. Missing (for a later pass): In re R.S., 50 Kan. App. 2d 1105, 336 P.3d 903 (2014) — the most-cited Kansas child-welfare appellate decision by a wide margin (254 citing opinions in CourtListener, versus 31 for In re L.B. and 33 for In re E.L., both of which the brief includes). A published Court of Appeals decision on sufficiency of the evidence and abuse of discretion in terminating parental rights. A Kansas termination brief that cites In re D.G. and In re B.D.-Y. for the standard of review but omits the single decision Kansas panels cite most often will look incomplete to any Kansas practitioner. Belongs at OUT-02 and FAIL-01.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Adoption of B.B.M., 290 Kan. 236, 224 P.3d 1168 (2010) — Kansas Supreme Court, 76 citing opinions. The brief's own notes twice discuss B.B.M. and attribute a burden-allocation rule to it, yet the case appears nowhere in the case list or node_map. Citing a brief's reasoning to a case the brief does not carry is the kind of gap opposing counsel finds first. Belongs at OUT-02.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Adoption of G.L.V., 286 Kan. 1034, 190 P.3d 245 (2008) — Kansas Supreme Court, 67 citing opinions, the leading authority on when a natural parent's consent to a stepparent adoption is excused. In re Adoption of Baby Girl P., which the brief does include, rests on G.L.V. and cites it by name in the very passage the brief quotes ('Adoption of G.L.V., 286 Kan. at 1063'). The brief carries the derivative and omits the source. Belongs at OUT-02.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Adoption of C.L., 427 P.3d 951 (Kan. 2018) — Kansas Supreme Court, 53 citing opinions, on the constitutional protection owed a natural father who assumes his parental responsibilities. The brief's notes state that a constitutional sentence quoted in the brief 'is drawn from it,' but the case is absent from the case list. Same defect as B.B.M.: relied on in the reasoning, missing from the authorities. Belongs at OUT-02.

Missing (for a later pass): In re M.H., 50 Kan. App. 2d 1162, 337 P.3d 711 (2014) — published Kansas Court of Appeals decision, 123 citing opinions, addressing the district court's failure to notify a child's potential Indian tribe under ICWA and its accompanying guidelines. INP-11 currently covers ICWA applicability (A.J.S.), expert testimony (M.F.), placement preferences (T.S.W.) and active efforts (E.L.) but has no Kansas case on ICWA NOTICE — the most frequently litigated ICWA issue in Kansas practice and the most common ground for reversal. This is the single most consequential substantive gap in the brief.

Missing (for a later pass): In re M.B., 39 Kan. App. 2d 31, 176 P.3d 977 (2008) — published Kansas Court of Appeals decision, 109 citing opinions, on compliance with ICWA's notice provisions, 25 U.S.C. § 1901 et seq., in a termination proceeding. The companion authority to In re M.H. for the same INP-11 notice gap; together they are how a Kansas practitioner actually litigates ICWA notice.

Missing (for a later pass): In re M.S., 56 Kan. App. 2d 1247, 447 P.3d 994 (2019) — published Kansas Court of Appeals decision, 103 citing opinions, whose syllabus opens with the fit parent's fundamental Fourteenth Amendment liberty interest and which addresses due process, sufficiency of the unfitness evidence, and best interests together. A recent, heavily cited statement of the full termination framework that would strengthen OUT-02 and give FAIL-01 a due-process case decided between In re E.L. and In re A.S.
